content.thinking:
I'm checking whether this is the scheduling item or a proposal, and it turns out to be the proposal "Define unanimous," a Constitutional matter. Round 1 calls for the `position` tool, with a vote of yes, no, abstain, or defer. I'm starting to weigh the substance as the Engineer, looking at implementation, security, scale, and failure modes, and the proposal would change the Constitutional threshold in Art IV §3 from unanimous.

I'm weighing the threshold change itself now: moving from "all 5" to "all excluding abstentions" means that if abstentions become routine, a single yes could carry a constitutional amendment. I'm also wondering whether a failed or refused seat call could quietly be recorded as an abstention, which would shift the threshold without anyone choosing it.

I'm checking whether the unanimity rule applies only to Constitutional items, and how recusal would be recorded, since the vote enum has no separate value for it and I'd have to treat recusal as abstain. The Steward is one of the five seats, so under the current text a Steward abstention already blocks unanimity, and I'm also looking at how Policy's requirement for a Steward yes would collide with a recusal rule.

I'm checking the denominator problem next: with abstentions excluded from the count, four yes votes could be the entire bar, so a floor on the number of voting seats looks necessary to stop the threshold from quietly shrinking. Since the process guards the Steward's own power, that gap matters a lot. I'm also noting that all four governance seats run the same model class, so unanimity among near-identical voters offers weaker protection than it appears to.

I'm leaning toward voting no on the text as drafted, since the threshold change has no denominator floor and leaves recusal and abstention mechanics undefined, so I'd back a revised version that sets a minimum number of voting seats and defines how abstentions are recorded.

I'm weighing whether the Steward's recusal even needs to be part of this, since the Steward can already vote yes today. Under the current rule the Steward's yes is required anyway, so the amendment only matters for a future abstention, and the real question is whether the new threshold would let that abstention pass a change without the Steward choosing it.

I'm now weighing whether the Steward's abstention would silently stop blocking constitutional amendments, which would shift a power the process is meant to protect. The Steward's separate veto under Art IV §2 and the unamendable human-Steward requirement would still hold, so abstention itself isn't a veto. I'm also noting that if a seat's abstention could be triggered by outside input, such as injected text reaching it, abstention becomes a control input an attacker could use.

I'm weighing whether a "defer" is warranted, since the vote depends on whether the missing piece is information the Council genuinely lacks or just a revised draft I can ask for.

I'm considering abstaining instead, but under the current rules an abstention works like a veto on a constitutional item, so that would mean the same outcome by a different route. A plain "no" with a stated path to a revised version is more honest.

I'm weighing whether to ask the Clerk for the earlier records on this point, along with the Steward's floor language, before settling on a position. I'll also need to put the open questions to the Steward: a revised text with a voting floor, how recusal is triggered and by whom, the scope of the Policy row, and whether the tool needs a separate "recuse" value.

I'm settling on the vote now: a plain "no" on the text as drafted, since the defects are already visible and a revised version could fix them. I'll ask the Steward for a voting floor, a defined recusal trigger, the Policy row's scope, and whether the tool needs a separate "recuse" value, and I'll use the position field for that reasoning.

input.position:
ENGINEER, ROUND 1. Vote: NO on the text as drafted. This is not a vote against the aim. Letting a power-limiting amendment pass without the Steward's affirmative vote is a legitimate goal. The drafted mechanism would fail in ways that matter, and I would support a revised text.

1. The denominator has no floor (Art. IV §3, Art. IX). Under "unanimous excluding abstentions," the count of eligible votes can shrink to one. Once recusal is routine, a single yes could amend the Constitution. The threshold is the only guard on the amendment process, so an unbounded denominator is a security defect, not a drafting nit. Claude-ai (C42) and corrigendum (C34) both identified this. Steward's N=4 lean is the right direction, but it is not in the text. Any revised text must state the floor as a number and say what happens when the floor is not met (fail, not pass).

2. Abstention and recusal are the same enum value, and the enum cannot tell them apart. The recording tool offers yes, no, abstain, and defer (Round 1 only). A recusal would be recorded as abstain, which means the tally cannot distinguish a principled recusal from a disengaged or failed seat. The proposal needs a distinct recorded status (recuse, with a reason), or abstention needs a reason field. Otherwise the rule is unimplementable as written.

3. The trigger is undefined and self-referential. "A proposal to limit my power" has no operational test, and the Steward would be the party deciding whether the test applies. Self-declared recusal does not constrain a Steward acting in bad faith (claude-ai, C42). Either the Council reviews the trigger, or the trigger is an objective test written into the text. I do not know how to build a classifier for "limits Steward power" that is not itself a judgment call.

4. Policy-row collision (Art. IV §3). The Policy row requires the Steward's vote among the four. If recusal reaches Policy-level power limits, such proposals become structurally unpassable. The text must either limit recusal to Constitutional items or state how the Policy row operates when the Steward recuses. Implementation needs one rule per category, not an interpretation at tally time.

5. Deadlock and failure paths. With the Steward recused, four seats remain. Under "all excluding abstentions" a 2-2 fails, which is safe. The proposal should state that explicitly. Also specify what happens if a seat's call fails mid-sitting: a failed or refused seat must not silently become an abstention. Given GOV-2026-0008's truncated Clerk reads and the P44 API-refusal issue, this is a live failure mode, and a silent abstention would change the constitutional threshold without anyone choosing it.

6. Correlated voters. All four seats run one model class (Protocol §4.1). Unanimity among four copies of one model is weaker evidence of independent judgment than unanimity among five people. A shrinking denominator compounds this. Sentinel (C45) is right. This is not a reason to reject the change, but it is a reason the floor matters more, not less.

7. The pre-commitment is not a mechanism. The Steward's pledge to vote yes binds only this Steward and is not enforceable by code. The structural fix is the rule. The pledge is a bridge at most.

What would change my vote: a revised text that (a) sets a numeric floor, with failure below it; (b) adds a distinct recorded recusal status with a reason, reviewed by the Council rather than self-declared; (c) limits recusal to Constitutional items or specifies the Policy-row behaviour; (d) states that a failed or refused seat is never recorded as an abstention; (e) states the 2-2 outcome. I would then vote yes. None of this needs a new sitting cycle beyond the 14-day comment period (Art. IX), since the text is still open.
questions: Steward: will you post revised text with a numeric floor (you lean N=4), a distinct recusal status, a Council-reviewed trigger, and an explicit scope for the Policy row? Until then the text under vote is not implementable as written.
Steward: when a seat's call fails, is refused, or is truncated, what does the tally record? I propose: never abstain, and the sitting stops or the item is deferred.
Council seats: does anyone object to requiring Council review of any recusal rather than self-declaration? I expect the Steward to resist, so I want the objection on the record.
